claim: Optimal decision-making relies upon accurate effort cost anticipation, which is generally assumed to be performed independently from goal valuation.
source: Optimal decision-making relies upon accurate effort cost anticipation, which is generally assumed to be performed independently from goal valuation.
evidence: This is a statement about standard decision theory assumptions presented in the abstract.

claim: Higher monetary prospects led participants to provide higher cost estimates, although reward was independent from effort in the experimental design.
source: Behavioural results show that higher monetary prospects led participants to provide higher cost estimates, although reward was independent from effort in our design.
evidence: This is the main finding from the behavioral experiments reported in the abstract.

claim: Prospective cost assessment is biased by the output of an automatic computation adjusting effort expenditure to goal value.
source: Among candidate cognitive explanations, they support a model in which prospective cost assessment is biased by the output of an automatic computation adjusting effort expenditure to goal value.
evidence: This is the conclusion from model comparison analysis presented in the abstract.

claim: This decision bias might lead people to abandon the pursuit of valuable goals that are in fact not so costly to achieve.
source: This decision bias might lead people to abandon the pursuit of valuable goals that are in fact not so costly to achieve.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential consequences of the observed bias.

claim: The subjective value of the goal is discounted by some function of the expected cost related to the energetic expense.
source: The general idea of decision-making theory is that the subjective value of the goal, defined as an anticipated outcome, is discounted by some function of the expected cost, related to the energetic expense (Chong et al., 2017; Hull, 1943; Kable and Glimcher, 2009; Klein-Flügge et al., 2015; Mitchell, 2003; Rangel et al., 2008; Schmidt et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work in decision-making theory.

claim: Most choice models assume that different costs integrated in the discounted value computation are estimated separately, following the independence axiom.
source: More generally, most choice models assume that the different costs integrated in the discounted value computation (not only effort, but also delay, risk, etc.) are estimated separately, a principle known as the independence axiom.
evidence: This describes a fundamental assumption in standard decision theory.

claim: Exerted effort inflates the perceived value of the associated outcome.
source: One line of research has described numerous instances in which exerted effort inflates the perceived value of the associated outcome (Arkes et al., 1994; Aronson and Mills, 1959; Inzlicht et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The IKEA effect causes individuals to ascribe greater value to an object that they assembled themselves compared to one assembled by an expert.
source: For example, yielding to the so-called 'IKEA effect' (Norton et al., 2012), individuals tend to ascribe greater value to an object that they assembled themselves compared to one that was assembled by an expert.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Norton et al., 2012.

claim: The value of the outcome modulates retrospective judgement about the amount of effort invested to reach it.
source: A distinct line of research has documented cases in which the value of the outcome modulates one's retrospective judgement about the amount of effort invested to reach it.
evidence: This is a summary of a line of research in the literature.

claim: People tend to incorporate the monetary reward into their retrospective judgement of effort intensity using the positive correlation between reward and effort in a Bayes-optimal fashion.
source: For example, people tend to incorporate the monetary reward into their retrospective judgement of effort intensity using the positive correlation between reward and effort in a Bayes-optimal fashion (Pooresmaeili et al., 2015; Rollwage et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pooresmaeili et al., 2015 and Rollwage et al., 2018.

claim: The planning fallacy is the tendency observed in healthy agents to underestimate the time necessary to complete a task or project.
source: The most widespread instance of systematic cost distortion is perhaps the 'planning fallacy', that is, the tendency observed in healthy agents to underestimate the time necessary to complete a task or a project (Brunnermeier et al., 2008; Buehler et al., 1994; Kahneman and Tversky, 1979), even when they have extensive experience about it.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on the planning fallacy.

claim: The planning fallacy occurs for other types of cost, such as money and effort.
source: While this fallacy has mainly been reported in the context of delay estimation, it also occurs for other types of cost, such as money (Peetz and Buehler, 2013; Peetz and Buehler, 2009) and effort (Morgenshtern et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on money and effort costs.

claim: The planning fallacy results from an excessive focus on the future goal, to the detriment of information accumulation about intermediate steps and declarative or experiential knowledge about the task.
source: The planning fallacy has been proposed to result from an excessive focus on the future goal, to the detriment of information accumulation about both the intermediate steps to be taken, and declarative or experiential knowledge about the task at hand (Buehler and Griffin, 2003; Kruger and Evans, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Buehler and Griffin, 2003 and Kruger and Evans, 2004.

claim: If more attractive goals capture more attention, then effort costs should be even more underestimated when the goal is assigned a higher value.
source: If more attractive goals capture more attention, then effort costs should be even more underestimated when the goal is assigned a higher value.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the attentional bias hypothesis.

claim: Participants tended to accept the high-effort option more often as the attached incentive level increased.
source: As illustrated in Figure 2a, participants tended to accept the high-effort option more often as the attached incentive level increased, and as the cost level decreased (with a sigmoid-like nonlinearity in the acceptance rate curve, characteristic of floor and ceiling effects for low and high differences between options, respectively).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Participants tended to accept the high-effort option more often as the cost level decreased.
source: As illustrated in Figure 2a, participants tended to accept the high-effort option more often as the attached incentive level increased, and as the cost level decreased (with a sigmoid-like nonlinearity in the acceptance rate curve, characteristic of floor and ceiling effects for low and high differences between options, respectively).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: After training, participants were able to estimate energetic cost of a running route with good accuracy (82% ± 3%).
source: Thus, after training, participants were able to estimate energetic cost of a running route with good accuracy (82% ± 3%), defined as the complement to distance from target (REC-AEC, see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a quantitative measure of participant performance from the experimental data.

claim: Participants tended to anticipate a higher energetic cost for better-rewarded running sequences, all other things being equal.
source: That is, all other things being equal, participants tended to anticipate a higher energetic cost for better-rewarded running sequences.
evidence: This is a restatement of the main finding from the GLM analysis.

claim: Prospective reward inflated AEC over and above choices made by the participants.
source: Therefore, prospective reward inflated AEC over and above choices made by the participants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analyses showing incentive effects independent of choice.

claim: Most healthy individuals hold the belief that obtaining more reward typically requires investing more effort.
source: First, given that most healthy individuals hold the belief that obtaining more reward typically requires investing more effort (Benabou and Tirole, 2006; Frieze and Snyder, 1980; Nalebuff and Stiglitz, 1983; Van-Yperen and Duda, 2007), our participants might have used the incentive cue as implicit evidence informing their effort cost estimation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on beliefs about effort and reward.

claim: The association between effort and reward levels is conditioned through reinforcement mechanisms according to the notion of learned industriousness.
source: This hypothesis is in line with a notion of learned industriousness, according to which the association between effort and reward levels is conditioned through reinforcement mechanisms (Eisenberger, 1992; Inzlicht et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eisenberger, 1992 and Inzlicht et al., 2018.

claim: Information about reward is likely to trigger an affective reaction from the viewer because of its personal relevance.
source: Second, because of its personal relevance, information about reward is likely to trigger an affective reaction from the viewer, as previously demonstrated in similar contexts (Knutson and Greer, 2008; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Knutson and Greer, 2008 and Wu et al., 2014.

claim: Affective states are classically parametrized in a two-dimensional space: arousal by valence.
source: In the psychology literature, affective states are classically parametrized in a two-dimensional space: arousal by valence (Posner et al., 2005; Russell, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Posner et al., 2005 and Russell, 1980.

claim: Both prospective and exerted effort has been shown to increase arousal.
source: In particular, since both prospective and exerted effort has been shown to increase arousal (Gellatly and Meyer, 1992; Schmidt et al., 2009; Varazzani et al., 2015; Vassena et al., 2014), it is possible that the cognitive system responsible for effort anticipation may use arousal state as one of its inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on effort and arousal.

claim: Prospective rewards increase arousal.
source: Moreover, because prospective rewards also increase arousal (Knutson and Greer, 2008; Wu et al., 2014), individuals might misinterpret incentive-triggered arousal as a cue about the upcoming effort, such that AEC would be higher when a higher reward is at stake.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Knutson and Greer, 2008 and Wu et al., 2014.

claim: It is well established that prospective reward positively modulates affective valence.
source: A similar reasoning could apply in a valence-based scenario since it is well established that prospective reward positively modulates affective valence (Knutson and Greer, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Knutson and Greer, 2008.

claim: Information about reward is a crucial input to the cost–benefit computations that adjust both the direction and intensity of behaviour, according to standard decision theory.
source: Third, at a motivational level, information about reward is a crucial input to the cost–benefit computations that adjust both the direction and intensity of behaviour, according to standard decision theory (Croxson et al., 2009; Glimcher and Fehr, 2013; Rangel et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to standard decision theory literature.

claim: The significant impact of gain level on AEC in Experiment 2, despite the demonstration that reward and effort were independent, contradicts one of the predictions of the 'belief' scenario.
source: The significant impact of gain level, despite the demonstration that reward and effort were independent, thus contradicts one of the predictions of the 'belief' scenario.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results in relation to the belief hypothesis.

claim: Prospective gains and losses inflated anticipated energetic cost over and above choices made by the participants in Experiment 2.
source: Therefore, prospective gains and losses inflated anticipated energetic cost over and above choices made by the participants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the statistical analyses showing incentive effects independent of choice in Experiment 2.

claim: Incidental arousal fluctuations do not affect anticipated energetic cost.
source: These observations suggest that incidental arousal fluctuations do not affect anticipated energetic cost, and therefore challenge the main prediction of the arousal variant of the 'affect' scenario.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the null results of the arousal manipulation.

claim: The lack of correlation between belief strength and incentive effects is in contradiction with one of the predictions of the 'belief' scenario.
source: This finding is in contradiction with one of the predictions of the 'belief' scenario.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the null correlation result in relation to the belief hypothesis.

claim: Both the 'maximal budget' and 'optimal expense' models predict the qualitative pattern observed in high-effort choice rate and AEC rating.
source: Both models do predict the qualitative pattern observed in high-effort choice rate and AEC rating.
evidence: This is a statement about the model predictions based on the model fits shown in Figure 6.

claim: This is the first time a positive impact of incentive magnitude on prospective effort cost estimates has been isolated in a controlled laboratory setting.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first time such an effect has been isolated in a controlled laboratory setting.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: The positive impact of goal value on effort cost estimates questions a fundamental axiom of rational decision theory, according to which effort cost and goal value should be estimated independently of each other.
source: It questions a fundamental axiom of rational decision theory, according to which effort cost and goal value should be estimated independently of each other.
evidence: This is an inference about the theoretical implications of the findings.

claim: The decision bias was observed irrespective of the reported belief in a general correlation between effort and reward.
source: Indeed, the decision bias was observed irrespective of the reported belief in a general (in real life) correlation between effort and reward, and despite the demonstration to participants that effort and reward were independently drawn at random (in the experiment), by playing lottery animations.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from Experiment 2 regarding the belief hypothesis.

claim: The decision bias was observed despite the demonstration to participants that effort and reward were independently drawn at random by playing lottery animations.
source: Indeed, the decision bias was observed irrespective of the reported belief in a general (in real life) correlation between effort and reward, and despite the demonstration to participants that effort and reward were independently drawn at random (in the experiment), by playing lottery animations.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from Experiment 2 regarding the belief hypothesis.

claim: Reward impacts prospective effort estimates that drive decision-making even when this influence is not instrumental.
source: Although such a Bayesian inference might be implemented in situations where it does produce valid conclusions, our results show that reward also impacts prospective effort estimates that drive decision-making even when this influence is not instrumental.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The impact of reward on effort cost estimates should be seen as an irrational bias, imposed by a cognitive process that is automatically triggered despite its irrelevance in the context of the experiment.
source: This impact should therefore be seen as an irrational bias, imposed by a cognitive process that is automatically triggered despite its irrelevance in the context of the experiment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in terms of cognitive mechanisms.

claim: The bias was not fully controlled since it occurred despite the monetary bonus offered for accurate judgements and despite evidence that reward magnitude and effort cost were independent from each other.
source: By automatic, we simply mean that the bias was not (fully) controlled since it occurred despite the monetary bonus offered for accurate judgements, and despite evidence that reward magnitude and effort cost were independent from each other.
evidence: This is an explanation of what is meant by 'automatic' in the context of the observed bias.

claim: The impact of incentives on effort cost estimates is unlikely to have been mediated by arousal state.
source: Thus, the impact of incentives is unlikely to have been mediated by arousal state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the null results of the arousal manipulation.

claim: Mediation by valence is unlikely because negative incentives (prospective losses) had the same impact as positive incentives (prospective gains) on effort cost estimates.
source: This mediation by valence is also unlikely because negative incentives (prospective losses) had the same impact as positive incentives (prospective gains) on effort cost estimates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the finding that both gains and losses increased AEC.

claim: The findings are in line with the predictions of the decision scenario, which assumes that participants automatically translate reward into effort.
source: Finally, our findings are in line with the predictions of the decision scenario, which assumes that participants automatically translate reward into effort.
evidence: This is a summary statement about which hypothesis is supported by the data.

claim: The ability to translate reward into effort would arise from the cost–benefit trade-off machinery responsible for the motivational control of behaviour.
source: This ability would arise from the cost–benefit trade-off machinery responsible for the motivational control of behaviour.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation for the observed phenomenon.

claim: Bayesian family model comparison provided strong evidence in favour of cost–benefit models, relative to purely descriptive, non-principled models.
source: Bayesian family model comparison across our two groups of participants provided strong evidence in favour of cost–benefit models, relative to purely descriptive, non-principled models (generalized linear regression).
evidence: This is a summary of the Bayesian model comparison results.

claim: Further comparison between the two variants of the decision hypothesis ('maximal budget' and 'optimal expense') did not suggest that one was more prevalent than the other in the sampled population of participants.
source: However, further comparison between the two variants of this hypothesis ('maximal budget' and 'optimal expense') did not suggest that one was more prevalent than the other in the sampled population of participants.
evidence: This is a summary of the Bayesian model comparison results.

claim: It is possible that both 'maximal budget' and 'optimal expense' mechanisms are at play within a given individual, either at the scale of a single-effort estimate, or across several estimates.
source: Besides, it is possible that both mechanisms are at play within a given individual, either at the scale of a single-effort estimate, or across several estimates, such that none of these mechanisms clearly dominates the other.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for why the two models were not distinguishable.

claim: Participants did not report performing cost-benefit computations during post-experiment debriefing interview, even when asked about a possible influence of monetary incentives on effort cost rating.
source: In any case, we must assume that these computations are implicitly performed by the brain because participants did not report them during post-experiment debriefing interview, even when asked about a possible influence of monetary incentives on effort cost rating.
evidence: This is a report of what participants said during debriefing.

claim: The computations underlying the decision bias are implicitly performed by the brain.
source: In any case, we must assume that these computations are implicitly performed by the brain because participants did not report them during post-experiment debriefing interview, even when asked about a possible influence of monetary incentives on effort cost rating.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the debriefing data.

claim: Prospective effort cost judgements are likely biased by the product of a prescriptive, decision-related cost–benefit computation.
source: The general conclusion remains that prospective effort cost judgements are likely biased by the product of a prescriptive, decision-related cost–benefit computation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the study.

claim: Higher evidence was found for models in which the probability of choosing the high-effort option was a function of anticipated effort cost rather than a direct function of real effort cost.
source: Indeed, we found higher evidence for models in which the probability of choosing the high-effort option was a function of anticipated effort cost (including distortions of the real effort cost by monetary incentives) rather than a direct function of real effort cost.
evidence: This is a result from the Bayesian model comparison analysis.

claim: Subjective distortions induced by goal value affect not only ratings of effort cost but also decisions about whether to exert more effort for a higher benefit.
source: This suggests that subjective distortions induced by goal value affect not only ratings of effort cost but also decisions about whether to exert more effort for a higher benefit.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the model comparison results.

claim: The decision bias makes ambivalent the role of goal value in expected utility computation: on the one hand, it increases the expected benefit of the action, but on the other hand, it also increases the perceived cost of the action.
source: In any case, this decision bias makes ambivalent the role of goal value in expected utility computation: on the one hand, it increases the expected benefit of the action, but on the other hand, it also increases the perceived cost of the action.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the implications of the decision bias.

claim: The net effect of the decision bias is to make high-value goals less attractive than they should be, if participants had not anticipated that they would come at higher costs.
source: The net effect of the decision bias is to make high-value goals less attractive than they should be, if participants had not anticipated that they would come at higher costs.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of the decision bias.

claim: Further investigation will be needed to assess the robustness and generalizability of these findings, circumscribe the scope of this phenomenon, and gain a fine-grained understanding of its computational and neural bases.
source: Although we think this work is an important step towards a mechanistic comprehension of how effort anticipation and other action-related judgements can interfere, further investigation will be needed to assess the robustness and generalizability of these findings, circumscribe the scope of this phenomenon, and gain a fine-grained understanding of its computational and neural bases.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: One remaining question is whether other types of prospective cost judgements, about mental effort in particular, are subject to the same distortions from goal value as were energetic cost judgements made about physical effort.
source: Specifically, one remaining question to be addressed is whether other types of prospective cost judgements, about mental effort in particular (but also delay or risk), are subject to the same distortions from goal value as were energetic cost judgements made about physical effort in our design.
evidence: This is a statement about future research questions.

claim: Because mental effort has been construed as a cost traded against potential benefits in decision-making models, we would expect the same decision bias: a cognitive activity would be anticipated as requiring more effort when it is associated to more valuable outcome.
source: Because mental effort has also been construed as a cost traded against potential benefits in decision-making models (Pessiglione et al., 2018; Shenhav et al., 2013), we would expect the same decision bias: a cognitive activity would be anticipated as requiring more effort when it is associated to more valuable outcome.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the current findings and prior theory, supported by citations.

claim: It remains to be tested whether the same bias would manifest in a scenario where no choice is made and participants solely report the anticipated energetic cost.
source: Besides, although it is unlikely that effort cost estimation occurs independently from decision-making in most real-life scenarios, it remains to be tested whether the same bias would manifest in a scenario where no choice is made and participants solely report the anticipated energetic cost.
evidence: This is a statement about a future research question.

claim: Earlier studies have reported a positive effect of goal value on force production, even when it is non-instrumental or in fact detrimental to performance.
source: In this study, the actual effort expended during running was controlled by the treadmill speed and slope. However, earlier studies have reported a positive effect of goal value on force production, even when it is non-instrumental or in fact detrimental to performance (Dam, 2017; Oudiette et al., 2019), which could indeed originate from a higher anticipated effort cost.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dam, 2017 and Oudiette et al., 2019.

claim: The positive effect of goal value on force production could originate from a higher anticipated effort cost.
source: In this study, the actual effort expended during running was controlled by the treadmill speed and slope. However, earlier studies have reported a positive effect of goal value on force production, even when it is non-instrumental or in fact detrimental to performance (Dam, 2017; Oudiette et al., 2019), which could indeed originate from a higher anticipated effort cost.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for findings from prior studies.

claim: In environments where the invested effort and the value of the attained goal are strongly correlated, information about this goal value is on average informative about the effort that will be required.
source: We can speculate that, in environments where the invested effort and the value of the attained goal are strongly correlated, information about this goal value is on average informative about the effort that will be required.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential adaptiveness of the bias.

claim: Using goal value as a heuristic for effort cost might help prepare the action, in situations where value is known with precision whereas information about the cost is more uncertain.
source: Thus, using such a heuristic might help prepare the action, in situations where value is known with precision whereas information about the cost is more uncertain.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential adaptiveness of the bias.

claim: A better preparation, for an overestimated difficulty, may later result in higher persistence towards high-value goals in the face of fatigue, pain, or other forms of adversity that might be encountered during action execution.
source: A better preparation, for an overestimated difficulty, may later result in higher persistence towards high-value goals in the face of fatigue, pain, or other forms of adversity that might be encountered during action execution.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential benefits of the bias.

claim: Overestimating the cost may lead people to abandon the pursuit of high-value goals that they actually have the ability to reach.
source: However, overestimating the cost may lead people to abandon the pursuit of high-value goals that they actually have the ability to reach.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential negative consequences of the bias.

claim: Missed opportunities due to overestimating costs may be particularly frequent in patients suffering from depression, who might be trapped in a paradoxical behaviour: ignoring attractive goals just because their high values are seemingly signalling high costs.
source: These missed opportunities may be particularly frequent in patients suffering from depression, who might be trapped in a paradoxical behaviour: ignoring attractive goals just because their high values are seemingly signalling high costs.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential clinical implications.

claim: The size of the effect was rather small in the experimental data.
source: We acknowledge that, even if it provides a well-controlled proof of concept, the size of the effect was rather small in our data.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment about the magnitude of the observed effect.

claim: The size of the effect critically depends on the specifics of the experimental situation, such as the range of incentive values that were proposed and the fact that participants were heavily trained to make accurate effort cost judgements.
source: Yet, this critically depends on the specifics of the experimental situation, such as the range of incentive values that were proposed and the fact that participants were heavily trained (and encouraged) to make accurate effort cost judgements.
evidence: This is an explanation for why the effect size might have been small.

claim: Further research is needed to investigate how preponderant the effect is in more naturalistic situations where people have only vague ideas about the actual costs.
source: Further research is needed to investigate how preponderant the effect is in more naturalistic situations where people have only vague ideas about the actual costs.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: A question for future investigation is whether the decision bias might manifest in the opposite direction when information about effort cost is available for a precise subjective estimate, while information about goal value remains vague.
source: Another critical feature of our design is that the incentive level was clearly indicated when ratings and choices were made, while the effort cost had to be estimated and memorized while viewing the running animation. A question for future investigation is whether the decision bias might manifest in the opposite direction when information about effort cost is available for a precise subjective estimate, while information about goal value remains vague.
evidence: This is a statement about a future research question.

claim: An opposite bias would result in overestimating prospective goal value when effort cost is obviously high and would lead people to another paradox: engaging in strenuous actions just because they seem costly enough.
source: This opposite bias would result in overestimating prospective goal value when effort cost is obviously high and would lead people to another paradox: engaging in strenuous actions just because they seem costly enough (to bring valuable reward, presumably).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a potential opposite bias.

claim: Twenty-two healthy adults participated in Experiment 1.
source: Twenty-two participants (10 females, 12 males; mean age = 25.6 ± 4.7 years) were thus recruited for experiment 1.
evidence: This is a description of the sample in Experiment 1.

claim: Participants in Experiment 1 received an initial endowment of 18€ and earned financial bonuses during the session, leading to a final payment of 30.7€ on average (SD = 4.5€).
source: Participants received an initial endowment of 18€ and earned financial bonuses during the session, leading to a final payment of 30.7€ on average (SD = 4.5€).
evidence: This is a description of participant compensation in Experiment 1.

claim: Twenty-four healthy adults participated in Experiment 2.
source: Twenty-four participants (12 females, 12 males; mean age = 26.0 ± 5.0 years) were thus recruited for experiment 2 and were all included in the analyses.
evidence: This is a description of the sample in Experiment 2.

claim: Participants in Experiment 2 received an initial endowment of 30€, which ensured a non-negative final payment, with a final payment of 41.8€ on average (SD = 4.4€).
source: Because participants incurred a risk of monetary loss during this experiment, they received an initial endowment of 30€, which ensured a non-negative final payment. This final payment was 41.8€ on average (SD = 4.4€).
evidence: This is a description of participant compensation in Experiment 2.

claim: The study was approved under reference C15-59 (ID RCB 2015-A01445-44) by the Ethics Committee for Biomedical Research of the Pitié-Salpêtrière Hospital.
source: The study was approved under reference C15-59 (ID RCB 2015-A01445-44) by the Ethics Committee for Biomedical Research of the Pitié-Salpêtrière Hospital, where both experiments were conducted.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the study.

claim: All participants gave informed consent prior to partaking in the study.
source: All participants gave informed consent prior to partaking in the study.
evidence: This is a statement about the consent process.

claim: Choice data from four participants in Experiment 1 were excluded before model fitting due to a total rate of 'no' choices ≤5/108.
source: Choice data (but not rating data) from four participants were excluded before model fitting due to a total rate of 'no' (resp. 'yes' for one participant) choices ≤5/108, that is, a percentage of 'yes' (resp. 'nno') choices >95%.
evidence: This is a description of data exclusion criteria in Experiment 1.

claim: Choice data from 10 participants in Experiment 2 were excluded before model fitting due to a total rate of 'no' choices ≤5/108.
source: Choice data (but not rating data) from 10 participants were excluded before model fitting due to a total rate of 'no' choices ≤5/108, thus a percentage of 'yes' choices >95%.
evidence: This is a description of data exclusion criteria in Experiment 2.
